doc.title: Mickey Roker interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Learning from the masters and finding your own voice
summary: He advises duplicating Clarke, Blakey, Papa Jo and Philly Joe until you find yourself, and not copying Gene Krupa or anyone exactly.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: And tell us for instance how you go about trying to accomplish that legato nature on a drumset.

You listen to the masters. You duplicate your masters until you find it yourself, until you get it. And then you can be yourself. But everybody comes from somewhere. The history, you know you listen to the guys that originated the stuff. Listen to Kenny Clarke, you listen to Art Blakey. You know what I’m saying? You listen to Papa Jo Jones. You listen to Philly Joe Jones. These are the guys that I like, that I listen to, to see just how they emphasize a phrase, you see what I’m saying? And to see how they just take two bars and make a phrase. And then you try to do the same thing. Because you don’t want to play the

same phrase — you might love him to death man, but you don’t want to play the same thing he played in the same places. It gets stale. Because jazz is not like that. I mean this, in the beginning when you were a kid and all the young guys wanted to play “Sing Sing Sing” like Gene Krupa. You know that was a show that you really listened to Gene and you’d say, “man I can play ‘Sing Sing Sing.’” But man you’ve got to get away from that. You’ve got to be yourself. You’ve got to learn how to express how you feel see and that’s what’s beautiful about jazz in comparison with other music. Other music you’ve got to be just like Bach or Beethoven or whatever you know? Okay we can be like Charlie Parker but we can also be like ourselves. And that’s accepted as long as you’re strong.
